title: Alkanes & alkenes
examples: What is the difference between an alkane and an alkene?
How do I test if an alkene is present in a sample?
Can you show me an example of an addition reaction?

explain.say: Today we will look at two types of hydrocarbons. These are alkanes and alkenes. They are both made only of carbon and hydrogen atoms.
Alkanes have only single bonds between their carbon atoms. Their general formula is n minus two plus two. This means C n plus two n minus two.
Alkenes have at least one carbon-carbon double bond. Their general formula is n minus two plus two. This means C n plus two n minus two.
Alkenes undergo addition reactions easily. This means they add atoms across the double bond. For example, ethene adds bromine to become 1,2-dibromoethane.
We can test for the double bond using bromine water. If an alkene is present, it will decolorize the brown bromine water. Alkanes do not react this way.
In everyday life, alkenes are useful for making plastics. For example, ethene gas is used to make polyethylene, which is used for plastic bags.

faq.q: How do I know if a molecule is an alkane or an alkene?
faq.a: You check the general formula. Alkanes have the formula C n H 2 n + 2, while alkenes have C n H 2 n. You can also look for a double bond in the structure.
asks: What is the difference in formulas?
How do I tell them apart easily?

faq.q: What does 'addition reaction' mean in this context?
faq.a: It means that atoms are added across the double bond. The double bond breaks, and two new single bonds are formed. This changes the molecule.
asks: What happens when it adds bromine?

faq.q: Why does bromine water change colour with alkenes?
faq.a: Bromine water is reddish-brown because of the free bromine molecules. Alkenes react with the bromine, using up the bromine and making the water clear.
asks: Does it mean the alkene is present?
Why does the colour go away?

faq.a: Yes, alkanes are called saturated hydrocarbons. This means they contain only single bonds, and they have the maximum number of hydrogen atoms possible.
asks: Do they have any double bonds?

faq.q: Can the bromine water test be used for other things?
faq.a: It is specifically used to test for the presence of carbon-carbon double bonds. It is a reliable test for distinguishing alkenes from alkanes.
asks: What else can I test for?

facts: Alkanes contain only single carbon-carbon bonds.
Alkenes contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond.
Alkenes react with bromine water by addition, causing decolorization.
The general formula for alkanes is C n H 2 n + 2.

quiz.why: Alkanes are defined by having only single bonds, which corresponds to the formula C n H 2 n + 2.

wrong.0: This formula does not represent a standard hydrocarbon type.
wrong.1: This formula suggests too many hydrogen atoms for the structure.
wrong.3: This formula is for alkenes, which contain a double bond.

quiz.say: When ethene reacts with bromine water, what happens?
quiz.why: The double bond in ethene allows it to react with bromine, removing the colour from the bromine water.

wrong.0: This would be the result if the substance were an alkane.
wrong.1: The reaction removes the colour, it does not change it to red.
wrong.3: This is incorrect; the reaction consumes the bromine colour.

quiz.say: A test tube contains a liquid that causes bromine water to lose its colour. What class of hydrocarbon is it most likely to be?
quiz.why: The ability to decolorize bromine water is the characteristic test for the presence of a carbon-carbon double bond found in alkenes.

wrong.0: This is a type of element, not a hydrocarbon class.
wrong.1: Alcohols react differently and do not typically decolorize bromine water.
wrong.3: Alkanes do not have double bonds and will not decolorize bromine water.
